PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Grade 5

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that informative writing teaches facts and narrative writing shares stories. But there is a third kind of writing — persuasive writing — where the writer shares what he thinks or believes about a topic. Today, I'm going to teach you how to recognize if a writer/author is sharing an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Unlike facts — which are right or wrong — opinions are neither. They are simply different. Two people can read about the same topic and arrive at completely different conclusions. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and argue why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse what the writer believes with fact. This gets trickier in fifth grade — because persuasive writing actually includes facts, details, and real examples. The writer is not teaching those facts — he is using them to convince the reader to agree with him. That means a persuasive piece can sound a lot like an informative piece. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes — and he is using facts to convince me." Then they can read and decide — did he convince you? Do you agree?

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes — it's informative writing. But remember — persuasive writing also includes facts. So if you see facts, don't stop there. Keep questioning the author's purpose.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings AND occasionally stating facts and details to support it? The facts are there to support the opinion, not replace it. Look for subtle opinion words and adjectives — words like "should/not, most, best, important, better, necessary, clearly." Could someone arrive at a different conclusion on this same topic? If yes — it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine whether the writer's purpose is to describe a narrative story, inform with facts, or persuade the audience with his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project End-of-the-Day Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "Students pack materials, record homework, and clean their workspace." That's what happens at the end of the day — fact. "Following these steps leads to a smoother end to the day." Everyone would agree with that. (Pause.) But persuasive includes facts, too. So I'm going to double check by asking another set of questions.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (Scan slowly, pointing to each sentence.) I don't see opinion words. The author isn't taking a side or arguing a position — he's describing a procedure everyone follows. (Shake head.) This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again; I'm going to determine the author's purpose for writing. Project End-of-the-Day Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) No character. Nothing happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "Students could spread out instead of crowding one area." Sounds reasonable. "A more relaxed setting can help students stay focused." That could be true. (Pause.) But just seeing facts doesn't mean this is informative. Let me think about this through the persuasive lens.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (Point to the first sentence.) "Allowing flexible seating during dismissal would create a calmer environment." Would everyone agree? Some might argue flexible seating creates more chaos, not less. (Point to the last sentence.) "Flexible seating would improve end-of-day routines." Improve — opinion word. Not everyone agrees on what improves dismissal. (Pause.) And look at how the facts work — "reduce noise and distractions," "help students stay focused." Those facts aren't teaching me about seating. They are supporting the opinion that flexible seating should be allowed. The facts are there to convince me. (Nod.) Could someone arrive at a different conclusion? Absolutely. This topic has different sides. Aha — it's persuasive!

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that indicate an author is sharing his opinion within persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project School Bus Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say no. Let's keep going.

2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Point to "Staying seated prevents injuries" and "Keeping noise levels low allows the driver to concentrate." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say those sound like facts — and they do. But remember — persuasive writing includes facts, too. Keep asking.

3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & with facts? Point to "Following school bus rules is necessary for maintaining safety." Would everyone agree these specific rules are "necessary?" Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Point to "Consistent rule-following helps protect all passengers." Does following the bus rules mean no one ever gets hurt? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. So what is this? Yes, persuasive!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Grade 5

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing isn't just about what you think — it's about what you can prove. But how do you know which side you can prove best before you start writing? Today, I'm going to teach you how to think through both sides of a topic to determine the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion you can prove. Writers don't pick a side right away and start writing. Instead, they determine the strongest side by carefully thinking through both choices before committing to one. The strongest side isn't necessarily the one you like best — it's the one you can best prove.

WHY the skill is important | If a writer picks a side too quickly — he may choose the harder side to prove. And "harder to prove" means exactly that: when he sits down to write, he can't think of what to say. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one that you have the most to say about. And in persuasive writing, it's all about convincing the reader, and you need A LOT of details to make your point.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at the persuasive topic and identify both choices. Don't lean either direction yet — just name them side by side and treat them equally.

Step 2: Zip it. Before thinking begins, run your finger across your lips — zip them shut. (Demonstrate the zipper gesture.) Your opinion is locked inside. It's not gone — it's just waiting. You are not allowed to unzip until you have thought carefully through BOTH sides. This is how writers avoid rushing to a decision.

STEP 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) A writer puts on the thinking cap of someone who genuinely loves this choice — even if he doesn't. (Teach students to use their hands & mime putting on a hat.)

To generate strong details, try these strategies.
• Picture someone you know who would love this choice. What would they say is great about it?
• Think small — don't just say "it's fun" or "it's good." Ask yourself: what exactly happens? What does it look, feel, smell, taste, or sound like? Small specific details are always stronger than big general ones.
• Think about what you've seen or heard — a commercial, a conversation, something a friend or family member said. That counts as thinking.

When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side. (Take off the blue hat and put on the red one.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice — even if it's not your favorite. Use the same three strategies. Give this side the same honest effort you gave the first one. Your zipper stays shut until you've done both.

This is how writers determine the strongest side — by thinking through both before choosing.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I do this.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: Would you rather stay up late or sleep in late? (Display the choices within a T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking yet — just naming them.

Step 2: Zip it. My first thought is already in my head. (Run finger across lips — zip.) Locked. Not saying it yet. I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on the Stay Up Late thinking cap. I'm going to think like someone who really loves staying up late.

I need to say more than "it's fun." What specifically happens? I need to think small. (Pause.) The house goes quiet. Not peaceful-quiet — completely-yours quiet. No one telling you what to do, what to watch, when to stop. You're in the middle of a game level you've been stuck on for days — and now you have all the time you need. You're watching a show that's normally off-limits on a school night. (Pause.) Think even smaller. What does that actually feel like? You're the only one awake. The whole house feels different this late at night — the sounds outside, the darkness, the stillness. There's something about being up when the world is asleep that feels almost like a secret.

Wow — once I started thinking small, the details just kept coming. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a stay-up-late person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves sleeping in. I'm a morning person — this isn't natural for me. I have to deliberately borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.)

Let me start small and build. No alarm, of course. But what does that actually mean? (Pause.) Your body wakes up on its own. No jolt, no scrambling. You open your eyes and the sun is already up — the room is bright and warm, not dark and disorienting. (Pause.) Think smaller. You're still under the blankets. You're not rushing to beat anyone to the bathroom. You feel fully-rested, that feeling that almost never happens on a school day. Breakfast isn't grabbed on the way out the door. Maybe I could even have brunch! The morning has a completely different rhythm.

Today, we are learning how to push ourselves past the obvious — to think small, think specific, and find the details that make both sides feel fully argued before we ever choose one.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: What is the best season — summer or winter?
2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) With the Summer thinking cap on, think small. What specifically do you wear? What does your body feel? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard shorts, T-shirts, bare feet — no coats, no boots, no layers. Just walk outside and go. Warm sun on your skin, grass under your feet, jumping into a cold pool when it gets too hot. (Hat off — students mime.) See how thinking about something as small as what you're wearing opened up a whole new layer of details?
4. Think like the other side. (Red hat on — students mime.) Put on the Winter thinking cap — even if summer is your thing. Think small. What specifically happens that makes someone love winter? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard sledding, seeing your breath in the cold air, hot chocolate warming your hands. Small details — both sides feel arguable now.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — pushing ourselves to think small and find specific details, even for the side we wouldn't naturally choose.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through both sides of this topic: Which is the best special — art or P.E.? When I project the topic, work with your partner to think of every small, specific detail you can for one side. Then switch hats and do the same for the other side. How many details can you two come up with? Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (2 of 2) — Grade 5

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Yesterday we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — putting on each thinking cap and pushing ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides. Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Yesterday you thought through both sides of a persuasive topic. But thinking alone isn't enough — ideas that stay in your head slip away before they ever make it into writing. Jotting captures each detail on paper during prewriting. Jotting means writing a concise phrase — 1-4 words to preserve the thinking without slowing down the process. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — Skill 1, Day 2. Review shortcuts and abbreviations.)

WHY the skill is important | A persuasive writer's goal isn't just to list details — it's to jot as many details for BOTH sides as he can think of during prewriting. This is critical to determining the strongest side.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart — blue hat side on the left, red hat side on the right. Both sides start equal.

Step 2: Zip it. (Zipper gesture — students mime.) Lock in your first instinct. Don't let it out yet. A writer who commits too early may miss the stronger argument entirely.

STEP 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat. Students mime.) Put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. Jot each detail in 1–4 words, on its own line, & stacking it down that side. Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow.

If you fill every line on that side before you're finished thinking — grab a second T-Chart and continue on the same side. The other side stays empty for now. Stay in that thinking cap until every detail is captured. (Remove blue hat. Students mime.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Jot each detail on its own line, stacking down that side. Give this side the same honest effort.

Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow down. However, sometimes while making the second list (Side B), the writer has a new thought for Side A. No problem. Jump over to Side A and jot it. Then return to Side B and continue listing details.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: Would you rather stay up late or sleep in late? (Display a blank T-Chart.) I write one choice at the top of each side. (Write Stay Up Late on the left & Sleep In Late on the right.) There — both sides are named.

Step 2: Zip it. (Run finger across lips — zip.)

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my Stay Up Late thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details for this side. Now I jot them — 1–4 words each, stacking down the left side. I'm not just writing "it's fun." I'm jotting the specific things that happen.

(Jot while narrating details.)
• Quiet house, completely yours
• Gaming — no one stops you
• Finish level — stuck for days
• Late shows — normally off-limits
• All alone — feels like secret
• Outside sounds, darkness, stillness

Once I started thinking small yesterday, the details kept layering. Now they're captured — nothing gets lost. (Take the hat off.) I think I'm done thinking like a stay-up-late person.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Hold up the red hat — don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves sleeping in & jot down the details. This is definitely harder for me because I'm such an early-morning person. But I'll think LIKE someone who loves to sleep in. (Put on the red hat.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under "Sleep in late." (Point at T-Chart.)

• I picture someone waking up when their body is ready — no alarm. (Jot: "no alarm.")
• Still warm under the blankets. (Jot: "warm blankets.")
• Sun already up — bright and cozy. (Jot: "sun up, cozy.")
• Full of energy because you actually slept long enough. (Jot: "full/energy — slept enough.")

(Pause.) Wait — I just thought of something for the Stay Up Late side. (Switch hats.) Being up when everyone else is asleep means you're totally on your own. You're in charge. I have to jump back to Side A and capture that before I lose it. (Jot "on own, in charge.")

OK — back to Sleep In Late. (Switch hats again.)
• No rushing to the bathroom, or to catch the bus. Even breakfast isn't rushed. (Jot: "no rush — bath, bus, brkfst.")
• Whole morning feels calm. (Jot: "calm.")

Today, we are learning how to jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about: What is the best season — Summer or Winter? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Point in the air — where do I write down the two sides, the two choices? Yes, Summer by the blue hat & Winter by the red hat.

2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.

3. Think like one side & jot. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — "no coats, no boots, no layers, warm sun on skin, grass under feet, jump/cold pool," etc.

4. Think like the other side & jot. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — sledding, hot chocolate warming your hands, seeing your breath in the cold air, etc. Does any of this make you think of another detail about Summer? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard some of you say that in the summer the air is hot, like a hair dryer blowing. (Switch hats & jot it.)

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for which is the best special — P.E. or art. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Grade 5

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has been prewriting — thinking through both sides and determining the strongest one. Today we transition from prewriting to drafting. The first thing a persuasive writer does in his draft is tell the audience which side he has chosen. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write a strong opinion statement at the beginning of any persuasive piece.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing begins with an opinion statement. The first sentence tells the audience exactly what the writer thinks and which side he has chosen. This is no longer prewriting — this is the moment the writer goes public with his thinking.

WHY the skill is important | Without a clear opinion statement at the opening, the reader has no anchor — he doesn't know what side the writer is on or what the writing is trying to prove. By stating the opinion first, the writer signals his position immediately and sets up everything that follows. Remember — the goal of persuasive writing is to convince the audience to agree. So get to the point fast.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled — the one with the most details and proof. The word or words labeling that side belong in your opinion sentence.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. This is typically found in the writing prompt. It's the broader subject the two sides come from — usually 1–3 words. It gives the reader context so the opinion doesn't appear out of nowhere.

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) By intermediate grades, writers rarely use "I think" or "I believe" in persuasive writing. Opinion language is much more subtle. It's drops a single word — like "should, clearly, or best" — rather than a sentence starter. Test out 3 different opinion words as options for the first sentence.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Combine all 3 items in one oral sentence: strongest side + bigger topic + opinion word. Try it different ways, each time using different opinion language. Listen for the version that is most direct, most confident, and most specific. The stronger and more precise that opening statement, the more confident and convincing the entire piece feels from the first sentence forward.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write. This is how all persuasive writing should begin — with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because." See SKILL #5 for where the "because" fits in persuasive writing.)

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I write an opinion sentence.

Step 1: Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled Sleep In Late — that's the side with the most details, the most proof. That's my strongest side. That's what my opinion sentence will be about.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. The full prompt that started all this was: "Would you rather stay up late or sleep in late?" I need to choose 1-3 words to include in the opening sentence. I could mention what the other side: "stay up late." I might also play around with "rather." That's 4 words, but it would provide the reader with a better idea of why I'm all of a sudden declaring that I like to sleep in late.

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Now I need to pick some opinion words. Let's try: should, clearly, best. I'll test these all out to see which one sounds the best.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Now I put the 3 pieces of information together — 1 of the opinion phrases plus the strongest side ("sleep in late") plus "rather, stay up late." I'll start with "should."
• "You should sleep in late, rather than stay up late." (Pause.) I've got the 3 pieces, but it sounds a little awkward bossy. It doesn't sound persuasive; it sounds demanding. Plus, I don't love using "you." Let me try a different opinion word — clearly.
• "Sleeping in late is clearly better than staying up late." (Pause.) I definitely like the word "clearly." It sounds very strong and authoritative. Let me dabble with "best" in a third attempt.
• "The best is sleeping in late, rather than staying up late." Huh, I don't like that one. It's very wordy. I'm definitely liking the second one I created.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. (Write slowly while narrating: Sleeping… in… late… is… clearly… better… than… staying… up… late.)

Today, we are learning how to write the opening opinion statement — the first sentence of any persuasive piece. Strong persuasive writing begins with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another one.
1. Determine the strongest side. Yesterday, we determined that Summer was stronger than Winter in the prompt: Which season is best?

2. Name the bigger topic. What 3 words from that full prompt do you think should be included? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several of you mention "season" for sure. Some of you might try using "best season."

3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the list of opinion words. Identify 3 you would like to play around with. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several possibilities. Let's go with "definitely, clearly, & most."

4. Put the 3 parts together. Let's start with "definitely." Put that with "Summer" and "season" or "best season." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "Summer is definitely the best season." What do you think? Is it strong or only okay? Why? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. OK, let's try an opinion sentence with "clearly." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "Clearly, summer is the best season." How does it compare to the first sentence? What is/is not working about the sentence? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. Let's try a third option using "most." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "Summer is the most enjoyable season of the year." Do you like this one better than the other two? Which is the best option and why? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on what is the best special — P.E. or Art? I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Name the bigger topic. 3. Choose 3 opinion words. 4. Put the parts together. 5. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Now it's your turn!
